title: Sixteen steps
hook: the breathing discourse gives sixteen steps in four groups of four

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eleven blessings, starting with sleep. Your line was kindness sleeps well. How did you sleep? Day one hundred and seven, and ten days with the breath begin.

Since you woke up this morning, you've breathed thousands of times, and you didn't have to think about a single one. Breathing happens whether you pay attention or not. And it only ever happens now. You can't take yesterday's breath, or tomorrow's. Maybe that's why the Pali texts give it a discourse of its own. It's number 118 in the Middle Length Discourses, the Anapanasati Sutta. And it takes something you do without thinking, and turns it into a whole path, in sixteen steps.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF BREATHS SINCE MORNING.` → `ONLY EVER NOW.` → `A WHOLE PATH IN SIXTEEN STEPS.`

segments.voice: Today's word is anapanasati. The standard explanation splits it in three. Ana: breathing in. Apana: breathing out. Sati: mindfulness. Mindfulness of breathing in and out. The discourse opens on a full-moon night at the end of the rainy season. Many monks are gathered, and the Buddha is so pleased with them that he stays another month. Then he teaches this. It begins simply. A person goes to a forest, or the foot of a tree, or an empty room. Sits down, legs crossed, body upright, and sets mindfulness in front. Mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. Then come the sixteen steps, in four groups of four. The first four are about the body: the long breath, the short breath, the whole body, calming the body. The second four are about feeling: joy, ease, noticing feelings, calming them. The third four are about the mind: knowing it, gladdening it, steadying it, freeing it. And the last four are about seeing clearly: change, fading, ending, letting go. Body, feeling, mind, and the way things are. That's a map of the whole inner life, and every step of it rides on one breath. The discourse makes a big claim: this simple practice, developed and made much of, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, and those lead on to awakening. Over the next ten days, you'll walk these steps a few at a time. They aren't meant to be finished in a week. But every step begins exactly where you already are: breathing in, breathing out. Sixteen steps, one breath.
screen: `ANA, APANA, SATI.` · `SIT, SET MINDFULNESS IN FRONT.` · `BODY, FEELING, MIND, SEEING.` · `EVERY STEP RIDES ON ONE BREATH.` · then, large: `SIXTEEN STEPS, ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit the way the discourse describes, as best you can: upright, but not stiff. Chair or cushion is fine. Let your attention rest at the front of the body, where the breath is easiest to feel: the nostrils, the upper lip, or the chest. Don't change the breath. Just know it. Breathing in, you know you're breathing in. Breathing out, you know you're breathing out. When the mind wanders, and it will, just come back to the next breath. If you'd like, try five minutes later today. The bell holds the time.
Anapanasati. Mindfulness of breathing in and out, taught in sixteen steps.
Your line: sixteen steps, one breath. Today, three times, stop and know one whole breath, in and out. Day one hundred and seven.

howItsDone: Anapanasati is taught in Theravada monasteries and in meditation centers in many countries, and practice begins with simply knowing the in-breath and the out-breath.

fork.setup: you're a monk, and the Buddha is about to teach mindfulness of breathing. where does the discourse say to begin?
options: in a forest, at a tree or an empty room, sitting upright.
fork.reveal: the discourse begins with the forest, the foot of a tree or an empty place: legs crossed, body upright, mindfulness set in front.

original.note: Pali: mindfulness (sati) of breathing in and out (ana-apana).

trapdoor: what you thought: a breathing exercise.
what it means: a path in sixteen steps that rides on the breath, covering body, feeling, mind and the way things are.
what a scholar hears: MN 118 maps the four tetrads onto the four satipatthanas; the old commentaries even disagree on whether the sutta's word assasa means the in-breath or the out-breath.

notes: MN 118 is paraphrased throughout; Chalmers' 1926 translation exists but isn't on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.

Editor review (days 95–112): cut the 'twenty thousand breaths a day' statistic and the hook's claim that breathing was the Buddha's practice on the night he awoke (not in MN 118, which is the only text cited); 'the one thing that happens' superlative removed; the ana/apana split is now 'the standard explanation', since the trapdoor itself notes the commentaries disagree about the breath words; cut 'many monks spend their lives with them' and 'one of the most widely practiced' in howItsDone.
Trapdoor: Visuddhimagga VIII reports that the Vinaya commentary and the Sutta commentaries take assasa (and passasa) in opposite senses; please check.
